Priors in mcp

Source: R/mcp-priors.R
mcp-priors.Rd

The prior argument of mcp() is a named list. Names are parameter names (cp_1, Intercept_1, x_2, sigma_1, etc.; see mcp-formula for how they arise) and the values specify their priors. Use prior_summary() to see the resolved priors of a fitted model, including defaults. See Working with priors for worked examples and prior predictive checks.

Details

Each value in the list is either

  • A distribution string (e.g., Intercept_1 = "dnorm(0, 1) T(0, )"). Distributions use JAGS names and argument order, including T() truncation, but with conventional scales instead of JAGS precision: SD for dnorm(), SD on the log scale for dlnorm() (sdlog in stats::dlnorm()), and scale for dt(), ddexp(), and dlogis(). Change points also accept dirichlet(alpha), and all priors accept data-dependent terms such as sd(y) (see below).

  • A numerical value (e.g., Intercept_1 = -2.1) fixing the parameter to that constant.

  • A model parameter name (e.g., Intercept_2 = "Intercept_1"), sharing that parameter's value. Note that reusing coefficients via same() in the segment formulas (e.g., ~ same(1)) is generally preferred. If two group-level deviations are shared via the prior, they will need to have the same grouping variable.

Regression priors

Weakly informative defaults are used where priors are not specified. These are the conventional defaults of rstanarm for intercepts and coefficients and of brms for scale parameters, with a few documented deviations. They are designed for stable estimation and prediction, but should be justified before hypothesis testing. Use prior_summary(fit, verbose = TRUE) to see the default priors of a model and the rules behind them. For more details, read the article on mcp default priors for all families, links, and distributional parameters, and for how the defaults deviate from rstanarm and brms.

Change point priors

Change points are always ordered: each change point keeps its specified prior, restricted to ordered change points. Use plot_pars(fit, prior = TRUE) to see the resulting marginal priors. The default is a flat Dirichlet prior on the segment lengths, written as dunif(min(x), max(x)) on each change point (read more). Set a minimum segment length using the previous change point in the lower bound, e.g., cp_2 = "dunif(cp_1 + 20, max(x))". Read more about setting priors on change points.

Notes on priors

  • Change point priors without dunif() or T() are truncated to the observed range of x, e.g., dnorm(30, 10) becomes dnorm(30, 10) T(min(x), max(x)).

  • Data-dependent terms: If mcp encounters a data-dependent term like min(time), max(time), mean(response), median(response), sd(response), or mad(response) in the prior string, they are resolved from the model data so a numerical value is passed to JAGS. The following terms are also allowed: n_segments() and n_cp(). The older constants MINX, MAXX, MEANX, SDX, MINY, MAXY, MEANY, SDY, and N_CP remain accepted with a deprecation warning.

  • Group-level change points: Group-specific change points follow a hierarchical normal distribution around their population-level change point, truncated so that they remain in the observed range and ordered. Read more.

  • Parameterization: Prior strings use conventional scale parameterizations. mcp converts these to the parameterization required by JAGS when generating code: inverse variance for dnorm(), dt(), and dlnorm(), and inverse scale for ddexp() and dlogis(). Use prior_summary(fit) for resolved priors and prior_summary(fit, verbose = TRUE) for their rules and descriptions.

See also

mcp(), prior_summary(), mcp-formula

Examples

model = list(
  response ~ 1,
  ~ 0 + time,
  ~ 1 + time
)
prior = list(
  cp_1 = "dunif(20, 50)",         # Distribution
  time_2 = "dnorm(0, 2) T(0, )",  # Truncated distribution
  Intercept_3 = 15,               # Constant
  time_3 = "time_2"               # Shared with another parameter
)
fit = mcp(model, data = mcp_example_data("demo"), prior = prior, sample = "none")
prior_summary(fit)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 5
#>   parameter   segment dpar  prior                  bounds                    
#>   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                  <chr>                     
#> 1 cp_1              2 NA    dunif(20, 50)          [20, 50], ordered         
#> 2 cp_2              3 NA    dunif(0.61863, 99.741) [0.61863, 99.741], ordered
#> 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    dnorm(13.825, 17.383)  none                      
#> 4 time_2            2 mu    dnorm(0, 2) T(0, )     [0, Inf]                  
#> 5 Intercept_3       3 mu    15                     none                      
#> 6 time_3            3 mu    time_2                 none                      
#> 7 sigma_1           1 sigma dt(0, 5.7, 3) T(0, )   [0, Inf]
